directions: Start seed indoors in warm conditions over a sterile, mineral cactus mix, and always source nursery-propagated seed or plants, since Chilean Copiapoa populations face heavy collection pressure and are protected under CITES Appendix I. A solitary, later clumping globular cactus develops a dense crown of golden-yellow spines radiating over a dark gray-green body, a striking color contrast that has made it one of the most sought-after Copiapoa in collections. Native to a narrow stretch of the fog-fed Atacama coast near Taltal, Chile, it depends on coastal camanchaca fog for much of its moisture and resents both summer humidity and winter wet. Grow in maximum sun with an unusually gritty, fast-draining mix and water only sparingly in the warmest months to avoid rot.

directions: Start seed indoors in warm conditions over a sterile, mineral cactus mix, and always source nursery-propagated seed or plants given the intense collecting pressure on Chilean Copiapoa in the wild. The gray-brown, turnip-shaped body sits nearly flush with the surrounding gravel and is topped by a woolly, spineless or nearly spineless crown, an adaptation that keeps most of the plant shaded and hidden below grade in its native desert pavement habitat. Native to the coastal Atacama region of northern Chile, it is exceptionally slow-growing even by Copiapoa standards and can take many years to reach a few centimeters across. Plant it slightly proud of the soil line in an extremely lean, fast-draining mineral mix, water only rarely, and provide full sun to keep the body compact.

directions: Sow seed indoors in warm, humid conditions over a fine mineral cactus mix; Frailea germinates readily from nursery-grown seed and is one of the faster cacti to reach flowering size. The small, glossy chestnut-brown to olive body is nearly spineless and usually stays solitary or forms only a few small offsets, staying compact enough for a windowsill collection of miniature cacti. Native to grassy, rocky habitats in southern Brazil, Uruguay, and northern Argentina, it produces small yellow flowers that most often stay closed and self-pollinate (cleistogamy), reliably setting seed even without full sun. Keep it in bright light with a fast-draining mix and water lightly through the growing season, letting the mix dry fully between waterings.

directions: Sow seed indoors in warm, humid conditions over a fine mineral cactus mix; like other Frailea species it germinates and matures quickly from nursery-grown seed compared with most miniature cacti. The tiny, dull green to brownish globose body is covered in small, comb-like spines pressed close to the surface and rarely exceeds an inch or two across even at maturity. Native to sandy grassland habitats in Uruguay, southern Brazil, and northern Argentina, it produces small yellow flowers that typically remain closed and self-pollinate, so seed-grown plants set fruit reliably even in a home collection. Grow in bright light in a fast-draining mineral mix and water sparingly, since the shallow root system is sensitive to prolonged wet soil.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in extremely fast-draining, mineral cactus mix, and source only nursery-propagated seed or divisions given heavy collection pressure on this CITES Appendix I species. Among the smallest Turbinicarpus in cultivation, its tiny, clustering gray-green body is covered in dense white, bristly spines that nearly obscure the surface, and it produces disproportionately large magenta-pink flowers each spring. Native to a narrow range of gypsum and limestone outcrops in Coahuila, Mexico, it is exceptionally slow-growing and prone to rot if overwatered. Use an especially lean, mineral mix, water only sparingly and infrequently, and keep it in a shallow pot that matches its diminutive root system.

The flattened, blue-gray, nearly spineless body closely resembles a small Lophophora, giving rise to its common name, though pale pink to white flowers with a darker midstripe reveal its true identity as a Turbinicarpus. Native to a small area of limestone desert in San Luis Potosi, Mexico, it grows very slowly and depends on sharp drainage to avoid rot during humid spells. Water sparingly and infrequently, provide maximum bright light, and use an especially mineral, fast-draining mix suited to its shallow, fibrous roots.

directions: Start seed indoors in warm conditions over a very lean, mineral cactus mix, and always source nursery-propagated seed or plants, since this slow-growing species is heavily collected from the wild and protected under CITES Appendix I. A broad, gray-green rosette of thick, triangular tubercles grows nearly flush with the ground, closely mimicking the surrounding limestone gravel of its native Chihuahuan Desert habitat in central and northern Mexico. A stout taproot anchors the plant through long droughts, and white to pale pink flowers open from the woolly, spineless crown in fall. Because it can take a decade or more to reach flowering size, use an unusually gritty, fast-draining mix, water sparingly even in summer, and expect a genuinely slow but very long-lived specimen.

Its elongated, yellowish-green, triangular tubercles spread outward in an open rosette that can eventually span close to a foot across, giving it a more angular, star-like silhouette than most other Ariocarpus. Native to limestone hillsides in Nuevo Leon and Tamaulipas, Mexico, it flowers in fall with pale yellow blooms opening from the woolly center. Grow in full sun with an especially gritty, fast-draining mineral mix and water only sparingly, since like its relatives it is extremely slow-growing and intolerant of wet soil.

Its narrow, upward-pointing tubercles form a compact rosette that closely resembles a small agave seedling rather than a typical cactus, a resemblance that helps camouflage it among succulent desert vegetation. Native to a single restricted area of gypsum soil near Tula, Tamaulipas, Mexico, it produces bright magenta-pink flowers from the crown in fall. Grow in full sun in an especially lean, fast-draining mineral mix and water sparingly, since it is slow-growing and, like other Ariocarpus, prone to rot in overly wet or humid conditions.

Unlike its rounded relatives, its body is reduced to a low, disklike center from which numerous long, spineless, tapering tubercles radiate outward like coiling snakes, an unmistakable form that gives the species its common name. Native to a small area of San Luis Potosi, Mexico, it produces pale yellow flowers with a reddish throat at the growing tip in warm weather. Grow in bright light to full sun in an especially gritty, fast-draining mix and water sparingly, since the unusual elongated tubercles are prone to rot if kept too wet.

This naturally occurring form of the bishop's cap lacks the flecks of white wool that dust the typical species, leaving a smooth, uniformly gray-green, five-ribbed columnar body that shows off its sculptural angles more clearly. Native to the same limestone hillsides of central and northern Mexico as the species, it flowers similarly with pale yellow, daisy-like blooms opening at the crown in warm weather. Water sparingly and let the mix dry fully between waterings, since despite its smoother look it shares the species' need for sharp drainage and minimal humidity.

directions: Sow seed indoors in warm, humid conditions over a very fine, sterile mineral mix, or better, obtain nursery-propagated grafted plants, since this famously minute species is difficult to grow on its own roots and is best kept grafted onto a more vigorous cactus stock. Reputed to be the smallest cactus species in the world, its soft, spineless, gray-green body rarely exceeds half an inch across and forms slow-spreading mats of tiny buttons in habitat. Native to sheer rock crevices in the high Andes of Bolivia and northern Argentina, it survives extreme drought by shrinking and hardening its tissue rather than storing large water reserves like most cacti. Keep it in bright, filtered light with excellent drainage, water only lightly, and avoid the deep soaking typical of larger cactus species.

Native to sheer limestone cliffs in Queretaro and Hidalgo, Mexico, it produces small white to pale pink flowers at the crown in spring. Grow in bright light to full sun in an especially gritty, fast-draining mix and water sparingly, since it is exceptionally slow-growing and easily overwatered in cultivation.

directions: Start seed indoors in warm conditions over a very lean, mineral cactus mix, and source nursery-propagated seed or plants rather than wild-collected material, since populations can be locally depleted by over-collection. The tiny, globose to cylindrical body is densely covered in short, chalky-white spines pressed flat against the surface, giving the whole plant a pale, button-like appearance that is nearly spineless-looking from a distance, and it eventually offsets into small clumps. Native to limestone gravel and rocky slopes from the Trans-Pecos region of Texas and southern New Mexico south through the Chihuahuan Desert of Mexico, it produces tiny pink flowers followed by slender red-pink fruits. Grow in full sun with an especially gritty, fast-draining mix and water only sparingly, since it is slow-growing and prone to rot in humid or poorly drained conditions.
